title: Vedic period: society and economy, early and later
seo_title: Vedic Period: Society, Economy and Early vs Later Vedic Age
meta_description: The Vedic period explained: dates, sources, society and economy, the shift from early to later Vedic times, and what archaeology and ancient DNA can tell us.
keywords: difference between early and later vedic period
summary: The Vedic period, roughly 1500 to 600 BCE, is the phase of north Indian history known mainly from the Vedas. The early Vedic age was pastoral and centred on the north-west; the later Vedic age moved into the Ganga plains, with settled farming, iron, larger kingdoms and a firmer varna order.

paras: The Vedic period takes its name from the Vedas, the oldest body of Sanskrit texts. Historians use them as their main source for north India between the end of the Harappan cities and the rise of the Mahajanapadas. The Rigveda is the oldest; the Samaveda, Yajurveda and Atharvaveda, together with the Brahmanas, Aranyakas and early Upanishads, are later. Our guide to the [Vedas and Upanishads](vedas-and-upanishads.html) explains how these texts are organised.

The dates are approximate. The Rigveda is usually placed around 1500 to 1000 BCE and the later Vedic texts around 1000 to 600 BCE. These dates rest on language, internal references and comparison with archaeology, not on any inscription. Some scholars argue for earlier dates; the ranges above are those used in most textbooks.

The world of the Rigveda lies mainly in the land of seven rivers, the Indus and its tributaries in present-day Punjab, Haryana and the north-west. Cattle were the main measure of wealth, and many hymns ask for cows, horses and sons. The word gavishti, a search for cows, is used for conflict.

Society was organised by kin. The basic unit was the family (kula), several families formed a village (grama), and larger groups were called jana or vish. The chief, rajan, led in war and protected the people, but assemblies called sabha and samiti had real influence. The varna terms appear, but mostly in one late hymn; birth-based caste was not yet rigid.
Farming existed, especially of barley (yava), but herding dominated. Trade was mostly barter, and there was no coinage.

In the later Vedic texts the centre shifts east, to the Doab between the Ganga and Yamuna and beyond. This matches the spread of Painted Grey Ware settlements found at sites such as Hastinapur, Ahichchhatra and Atranjikhera. Iron, called shyama ayas or krishna ayas, appears in texts and excavations, and helped in tools and weapons, though how far it drove forest clearance is debated.

Settled agriculture became the base of the economy, with rice, wheat and barley. Larger territorial units called janapadas formed, rajas became more powerful, and elaborate sacrifices such as the rajasuya and ashvamedha displayed royal authority. The sabha and samiti lost weight. The four varnas became more clearly ranked and tied to birth, and the status of women narrowed compared with the earlier texts.

sections.h2: Where did the Vedic people come from? The evidence and the debate
paras: This is one of the most argued questions in Indian history, and the evidence comes from three directions. Linguists note that Sanskrit belongs to the Indo-European family and is closely related to Avestan, the language of early Iran. Archaeologists look for material traces of horses, chariots and burial practices. Geneticists now study ancient DNA.

One group of scholars holds that speakers of Indo-Aryan languages entered South Asia from Central Asia during the 2nd millennium BCE, in gradual movements rather than a single invasion, and mixed with existing populations. Ancient DNA studies published since 2018, including work on a Rakhigarhi burial, have found steppe-related ancestry arriving in South Asia in this period and absent from the Harappan individuals sampled. Another group argues that Vedic culture developed within India, and reads the same evidence as continuity from Harappan times.

The old idea of a violent Aryan invasion that destroyed Harappan cities is not supported by archaeology and has been set aside by most researchers. Beyond that, a fair summary is that the genetic data point to population movement and mixing, while the precise link between genes, languages and the Vedic texts is still being worked out. Our session on [ancient DNA and the Harappan debate](ancient-dna-and-the-harappan-debate.html) lays the studies side by side so students can read them for themselves.

sections.h2: Seeing the Vedic period through objects
paras: The Vedic period has no grand monuments, so it is best approached through pottery, metal and texts. A [museum morning with an archaeologist](museum-morning-with-an-archaeologist.html) can include Painted Grey Ware and Chalcolithic material alongside the Harappan gallery, and a [pottery workshop](clay-and-the-past-a-pottery-workshop.html) shows how archaeologists tell one ware from another. For what came next, read our guides to the [Indus Valley Civilization](indus-valley-civilization.html) and the [Indian history timeline](indian-history-timeline.html).

faq.q: What is the time period of the Vedic age?
faq.a: The Vedic age is usually dated to about 1500 to 600 BCE. The early Vedic or Rigvedic period runs from about 1500 to 1000 BCE, and the later Vedic period from about 1000 to 600 BCE. These dates are approximate and some scholars propose earlier ones.

faq.q: What was the main occupation in the early Vedic period?
faq.a: Cattle-rearing was the main occupation in the early Vedic period. Cows were the chief form of wealth and appear constantly in the Rigveda. Barley was cultivated, but agriculture became the backbone of the economy only in the later Vedic period.

Sabha and samiti were assemblies in Vedic society. The sabha was probably a smaller council of elders and the samiti a broader assembly of the people. Both advised and checked the rajan in the early Vedic period, and declined in importance as kingship grew stronger later.

faq.q: Which pottery is linked with the later Vedic period?
faq.a: Painted Grey Ware, a fine grey pottery painted with black designs, is linked with the later Vedic period in the Ganga-Yamuna Doab. It is found at sites such as Hastinapur, Ahichchhatra and Atranjikhera, roughly from the late 2nd millennium to the mid 1st millennium BCE.

faq.q: Was there an Aryan invasion of India?
faq.a: Most historians and archaeologists no longer accept the idea of a violent invasion that destroyed Harappan cities. Many hold that Indo-Aryan speakers arrived through gradual migration and mixing, supported by recent ancient DNA studies; others argue for an indigenous origin. The details remain under study.

posts.hook: In the Rigveda, a word for war meant searching for cows.
posts.caption: Gavishti, the search for cattle, shows how central herds were to early Vedic life. Settled farming took over only in later Vedic times.

posts.hook: Looking for the Vedic period in a museum? Look for grey pots.
posts.caption: Painted Grey Ware, thin grey pottery with black designs, is the archaeological marker most linked to later Vedic settlements in the Ganga-Yamuna Doab.
